subject: Extracting rows of a matrix according to another matrix

messages.author: 909ff578d0e714f8
messages.subject: Extracting rows of a matrix according to another matrix
parts:
Hi everyone,

I would like to perform matrix the multiplication Z %*% A where:
A is pxp,  Z is nxp sparse matrix of 0/1 entries, n>>p.

The usual operation (%*% or crossprod()) is very inefficient and slow when n is big (say, 10^4). I wanted to take advantage of the structure of Z to speed up the computation.
Suppose, for example, that Z is

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    0    0
[2,]    1    0    0
[3,]    0    1    0
[4,]    0    1    0
[5,]    0    0    1
[6,]    0    0    1

Then the first row of the product Z %*% A is the first row of A, the second row is the first row of A, the third row is the second row of A, and so on. 
What is an efficient way of extracting the rows of A accordingly?

Thank you!!

Asaf

messages.author: 9d7c257e609d0807
messages.subject: Re: [Israel RUG] Extracting rows of a matrix according to another matrix
parts:
I'm not sure I understand the question. but here are a few shots that might be helpful.
first, if z = Z[i,] for some i,

then your i'th row should be:
colSums(A[as.logical(z),])
I'm not sure if this is fast enough. it certainly doesn't fully exploit the fact that Z is sparse.
the full algorithm would be:

result = t(apply(z,1,function(x) colSums(A[as.logical(x),,drop=F])))
not sure if it is faster than direct multiplication though.

however, you may be able to extract the column location of the 1's in each row quite easily from the internal representation of z. in that case, instead of "as.logical(x)", you put something that has the meaning of "which(x==1)" that is easily computed.

also, an important tip - instead of extracting rows, try to work with columns. column extraction is faster than row extraction in many cases. just compute t(A)%*%t(Z) instead of Z%*%A

one last tip: you said n>>p. however, if n>>2^p (or if, for whatever reason, there are lots of repeating rows in Z), then you should consider precomputing the sum of all potential row combinations of A (which are potential rows in the outcome), and then just selecting them using a simple index. in this case you are computing only 2^p combinations instead of n combinations.

to convert a row (of Z) to an index just compute:
z.row.index = 1+ Z%*%(2^(0:(ncol(z)-1)))

and make sure that length(unique(z.row.index)) is indeed significantly less than nrow(Z)

HTH

amit

Asaf
